clue.text: Stick man in heart of heart

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is enclosed by it, so the man goes inside

blocks.note: the core is the heart of an apple or of a matter
a man is referred to as he

explanation.surface: A wooden figure lodged in someone's chest, like a voodoo doll pin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heart of heart' reads as an emotional phrase; the first 'heart' is the word clued and 'of heart' just restates it as the centre of things.
explanation.definitionFit: To cohere is to hold together, as things that stick to one another do.

clue.text: The dog on the right is one of mine

blocks.note: a collie is a sheepdog breed
R is the usual abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Pointing out a dog standing to the right and claiming it as one's own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One of mine' sounds possessive, but it means a worker in a coal mine.
explanation.definitionFit: A collier works underground digging coal, so he belongs to a pit or colliery.

clue.text: Agreement to follow Henry, king of the free market

indicators.note: placing something to follow another puts it directly after it in the answer

blocks.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
aye is a yes vote
K is king in chess notation

explanation.surface: A deal following a monarch, describing a champion of free-market economics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King' does double work: it gives K and also makes Hayek the king of the free market. Friedrich Hayek was the Austrian economist who championed free markets.
explanation.definitionFit: Friedrich Hayek was the leading twentieth-century economist arguing for unregulated markets over central planning.

clue.text: Polish and half Hungarian city turning up on a roll

indicators.note: half a name keeps only one of its two parts
in a down entry, turning up means reading from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: to polish is to rub
Budapest is made of Buda and Pest; the first half is taken

explanation.surface: Shining shoes and a trip to half of Budapest while on a lucky streak.
explanation.walkthrough: Polish looks like the nationality but is the verb. A rub-a-dub is the sound of a drum roll.
explanation.definitionFit: Rub-a-dub imitates the beating of a drum, as heard during a drum roll.

clue.text: Trouble with French umpires?

blocks.note: Fr is the abbreviation for French
ACAS is Britain's Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service, which arbitrates labour disputes

explanation.surface: Bother caused by referees in France.
explanation.walkthrough: ACAS is the UK body that steps in as umpire in industrial disputes, a piece of British knowledge.
explanation.definitionFit: A fracas is a noisy quarrel or brawl, which is a kind of trouble.

clue.text: The groove should be discounted

definitions.note: a verb phrase: to rebate is to give a discount, so this reads as the verb with 'should be'

blocks.note: first meaning: a step-shaped channel cut along a board edge, also called a rabbet
second meaning: to give money back off a price

explanation.surface: A rhythm or rut that ought to be written off.
explanation.walkthrough: The joinery sense is less familiar: a rebate is a recess cut along an edge to take another piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Rebate is both a carpentry recess and a partial refund, so it serves for both a cut channel and money given back.

clue.text: Austrian region (not Greek): hint - blended into part of Asia Minor

indicators.note: things blended are mixed together, so the letters lose their order
putting something into another places it inside that other

blocks.note: taken as written, for mixing
Caria was an ancient region in the south-west of Asia Minor

explanation.surface: A geography note stressing that an Austrian province is not to be confused with somewhere Greek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not Greek' warns off Corinthia, the Greek region around Corinth, which differs by one letter. Carinthia is Kärnten, Austria's southernmost state.
explanation.definitionFit: Carinthia is a federal state in southern Austria, bordering Italy and Slovenia.

clue.text: Cat and dog turn up mates round the field, he wrote amusingly

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning up means the letters read from the bottom upwards
the mates go round, surrounding the field between them

blocks.note: cats and dogs are household pets
a hen and a cock are mates, split either side
lea is a poetic word for a meadow

explanation.surface: Pets bounding across a field to meet their partners, described by a comic writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cat and dog' covers PETS together, not two separate words. Stephen Leacock was a Canadian humorist of the early twentieth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Leacock was a famous Canadian humorist, author of comic sketches such as Literary Lapses.

clue.text: A prize for crazy nut Curtis: did he get it for needlework?

definitions.text: did he get it for needlework

indicators.note: something crazy is disordered, so these letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
a cup is a trophy awarded as a prize
taken as written, for scrambling

explanation.surface: Wondering whether an eccentric called Curtis won an award for his sewing.
explanation.walkthrough: Needlework suggests sewing or embroidery; here it is the needles of Chinese medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: An acupuncturist treats patients by inserting fine needles, so his work is literally needle work.

clue.text: See 25
See 12
Which is the more offputting? Defeated addiction (turning light on, note) to cannabis, or  ...

definitions.note: the phrase means put off, so 'offputting' is the act it names

indicators.note: turning words over churns their order, so the bracketed letters are rearranged

blocks.note: to kick a habit is to beat an addiction
taken as written, for rearranging
grass is slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: Asking which is worse: a reformed addict lighting up a joint, or some oddly named person.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on into 12, so the question compares two idioms for postponing. The bracket looks like stage directions but holds the rearranged letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To kick a matter into the long grass is to shelve it indefinitely, which is putting it off.

clue.text: ... Don Renrub?

definitions.note: the whole clue is read cryptically; the sense of postponing comes from 'offputting' in 11

blocks.note: surface reading: a gentleman with an odd surname, offered as the second option in 11's question
setter's reading: don means put on, and Renrub is a kitchen word for a hob ring written back to front, so it sits on the back

explanation.surface: The second option in 11's question, a man oddly named Don Renrub.
explanation.walkthrough: This completes 11's question, whose 'offputting' covers both idioms. Renrub reversed is the cooker ring, so the name is a picture of putting on the back one.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting something on the back burner means postponing it, the same offputting as kicking it into long grass.

clue.text: Money not allowed, they say, for semi-military sound

indicators.note: what they say is heard spoken, so the word is matched by its sound

blocks.note: brass is British slang for money
banned means not allowed

explanation.surface: Cash being forbidden, rumour has it, to pay for some marching music.
explanation.walkthrough: Brass for money is northern English slang ('where there's muck there's brass').
explanation.definitionFit: Brass bands grew from military and colliery bands, playing marches with a quasi-military sound.

clue.text: Wader used by cockney woodworker?

indicators.note: a cockney pronounces long a like a long i, so the word is heard in that London accent

blocks.note: abrasive paper, the woodworker's smoothing sheet, as a Londoner says it

explanation.surface: Asking whether an East End carpenter would use a long boot for wading.
explanation.walkthrough: A cockney is a working-class Londoner, whose 'paper' sounds like 'piper'. 'Woodworker' is not a person here but the thing that smooths wood.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandpiper is a small wading bird found on shores and mudflats.

clue.text: See 25
See 11
See 7
St Francis could see all right, still keeping one genetically modified

indicators.note: one thing keeping another holds it within itself

blocks.note: static means motionless
I is the Roman numeral one
GM is the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A saint whose eyesight was fine, still holding on to some modified crop.
explanation.walkthrough: St Francis of Assisi bore the stigmata, Christ's wounds. Someone astigmatic cannot see straight, so dropping the A gives someone who sees all right.
explanation.definitionFit: Stigmatic names one marked with the stigmata, as Francis was, and jokingly the opposite of astigmatic eyesight.

clue.text: Like the 23 on the other side, on return of French boy to work

definitions.text: Like the 23 on the other side

indicators.note: something on its return comes back the way it went, so these letters run backwards

blocks.note: René is a French boy's name
the erg is a unit of work in physics

explanation.surface: Something across the way looks better, as a French lad comes back to his job.
explanation.walkthrough: 23 is GRASS, and the proverb says the grass is always greener on the other side of the fence.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb holds that grass on the other side always seems greener, so this completes it.

clue.text: See 11
Don't go straight to the southwest - veer off

indicators.note: letters gone off are out of order, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: SW is the compass abbreviation
taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: Directions telling a driver to bend south-westwards rather than keep straight on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Veer off' looks like the definition of turning aside; the definition is at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To swerve is to deviate suddenly from a straight course.

clue.text: How many people do you need for open war? A thousand?

definitions.text: How many people do you need

indicators.note: the question mark flags that the words are not to be taken straight but rearranged

blocks.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: A general asking how big an army must be to fight openly, perhaps a thousand men.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no explicit mixing word; the letters of 'open war' must be rearranged after M, the thousand placed first.
explanation.definitionFit: Manpower is the number of workers or soldiers available or required for a task.

clue.text: Stature, top to toe, of King Henry?

indicators.note: moving from top to toe sends the first letter down to the end

blocks.note: stature is a person's height

explanation.surface: Wondering how tall Henry VIII was from head to foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top to toe' reads as measuring someone's height; it is the instruction to move the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry the Eighth: the ordinal names which King Henry is meant.

clue.text: See 11
Capital in almost vulgar likeness

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so a letter is dropped
something in another sits inside it

blocks.note: Paris is the French capital
common means coarse or vulgar

explanation.surface: A city depicted in a crude, nearly vulgar picture.
explanation.walkthrough: One M is dropped from COMMON and the capital goes in the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: A comparison points out a likeness between things, as in 'there is no comparison'.

clue.text: An inclination by respected colleague with half the choir at a time

definitions.text: half the choir at a time

blocks.note: taken as written
a tip is a tilt or inclination
Hon is short for Honourable, a title of respect
an ally is an associate or colleague

explanation.surface: A slant offered by a valued colleague who sings with half of a choir.
explanation.walkthrough: Antiphonal singing alternates between two halves of a choir, each answering the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Antiphonally describes singing in alternate responses between two groups, so each half of the choir sings in turn.

clue.text: The heart has a military sound

indicators.note: the sound of a word is how it is heard, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: a colonel is a military officer

explanation.surface: The heart beats with a drumlike, marching rhythm.
explanation.walkthrough: Colonel and kernel are pronounced alike, despite the very different spellings.
explanation.definitionFit: The kernel is the central, essential part of something, like a seed within a nut.

clue.text: He set course for a desert island

definitions.text: He set course for a desert island

indicators.note: to set something is to arrange it, so these letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: taken as written, for rearranging

explanation.surface: A sailor plotting a voyage to an uninhabited island.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes Defoe's castaway, while 'course' rearranged spells his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Robinson Crusoe, Defoe's hero, sailed and was shipwrecked on a desert island.
